title: The hallmarks of cancer
blurb: The shared abilities cancer cells pick up, shown inside the cell.

text.simple: Scientists noticed that almost all cancers gain the same set of 'superpowers'. They called them the **hallmarks of cancer**.
text.student: In 2000, Douglas Hanahan and Robert Weinberg proposed that cancers share a small set of acquired capabilities, the **hallmarks**. The list was expanded in 2011 and 2022. [@hanahan2000] [@hanahan2011] [@hanahan2022]
text.deep: The hallmarks framework organizes tumor biology into acquired capabilities (sustained proliferative signaling, evading growth suppressors, resisting cell death, replicative immortality, angiogenesis, invasion/metastasis, deregulated metabolism, immune evasion) plus enabling characteristics such as genome instability and tumor-promoting inflammation. [@hanahan2011] [@hanahan2022]

text.simple: Cancer cells give themselves their own 'go' signal, like a gas pedal glued down.
text.student: **Sustained proliferative signaling:** mutations in genes like **KRAS** or fusions like **BCR-ABL1** (in K562) keep growth signals switched on with no outside input. [@hanahan2011]
text.deep: Constitutive activation of RTK/RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling, via activating mutations, amplifications or fusions, decouples proliferation from mitogen availability. [@hanahan2011]

text.simple: Cells have brakes that say 'stop dividing!' Cancer cells break them.
text.student: **Evading growth suppressors:** tumor suppressors like **RB** and **p53** normally stop division. Cancers often lose them. K562 has lost p53. [@hanahan2011] [@law1993]
text.deep: Loss of RB pathway control (RB1, CDKN2A) and p53 function removes checkpoints at G1/S and after DNA damage. [@hanahan2011]

try.note: MCL1 is an anti-death protein on mitochondria. Here are the measured effects of knocking it down.

text.simple: Damaged cells normally destroy themselves to protect the body. Cancer cells switch off this self-destruct button.
text.student: **Resisting cell death:** proteins like **MCL1** and **BCL-XL** guard the mitochondria against apoptosis (programmed cell death). Cancers often make extra of them. [@hanahan2011]
text.deep: Upregulation of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members (BCL-2, BCL-XL, MCL1) prevents BAX/BAK-mediated mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and cytochrome c release. [@hanahan2011]

text.simple: Normal cells can only divide a limited number of times, like a countdown. Cancer cells reset the countdown.
text.student: **Replicative immortality:** chromosome tips (telomeres) shorten with each division. Cancer cells switch on the enzyme **telomerase** to rebuild them. (RPE1 cells were given telomerase on purpose so they'd keep growing in the lab.) [@hanahan2011] [@bodnar1998]
text.deep: Telomere maintenance by TERT reactivation (or ALT) bypasses replicative senescence and crisis. Note that RPE1's hTERT immortalization means it shares this one hallmark with cancer cells. [@bodnar1998]

text.simple: Cancer cells change how they eat and make energy, so they can build new cells fast.
text.student: **Deregulated metabolism:** many cancer cells burn sugar in an unusual way (the 'Warburg effect') to get building blocks for new cells. [@vanderheiden2009]
text.deep: Aerobic glycolysis and rewired anabolic metabolism support biomass production for proliferation; mitochondria remain important for biosynthesis and redox balance. [@vanderheiden2009]

text.simple: Cancers also grow their own blood supply, spread to other places, and hide from the immune system. Those happen between cells, so our single-cell view can't show them.
text.student: Other hallmarks include **inducing blood vessel growth**, **invading and spreading** (metastasis), and **evading the immune system**. These involve the tissue around the tumor, which a single cell in a dish can't show. [@hanahan2011]
text.deep: Angiogenesis, invasion/metastasis and immune evasion depend on the tumor microenvironment and are not captured in monoculture cell-line screens, an important limit of this tool. [@hanahan2022]
